specStatements.text: Mains electricity is an ac supply. In the United Kingdom the domestic electricity supply has a frequency of 50 Hz and is about 230 V.
Students should be able to explain the difference between direct and alternating potential difference.
Most electrical appliances are connected to the mains using three-core cable.
The insulation covering each wire is colour coded for easy identification:
earth wire – green and yellow stripes.
The live wire carries the alternating potential difference from the supply. The neutral wire completes the circuit. The earth wire is a safety wire to stop the appliance becoming live.

The potential difference between the live wire and earth (0 V) is about 230 V. The neutral wire is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V). The earth wire is at 0 V, it only carries a current if there is a fault.
Students should be able to explain:
• that a live wire may be dangerous even when a switch in the mains circuit is open
• the dangers of providing any connection between the live wire and earth.

concepts.definition: A potential difference that repeatedly changes direction, so the current it drives repeatedly reverses direction round the circuit. Mains electricity is an ac supply.
A potential difference that is always in the same direction, so the current it drives passes round the circuit in one direction only. Cells and batteries supply a direct potential difference.
The ac supply delivered to homes in the United Kingdom: a frequency of 50 Hz and a potential difference of about 230 V.
The number of complete cycles of an alternating supply each second, measured in hertz (Hz). A 50 Hz supply completes 50 cycles every second.
The cable used to connect most electrical appliances to the mains. It contains three wires: live, neutral and earth.
The brown wire, which carries the alternating potential difference from the supply. It is at about 230 V relative to earth.
The blue wire, which completes the circuit. It is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V).
The green and yellow striped wire. It is a safety wire, at 0 V, which stops the appliance becoming live; it only carries a current if there is a fault.
The potential of the ground, taken as 0 V. The potential difference between the live wire and earth is about 230 V, which is why any connection from live to earth is dangerous.
The insulation covering each wire is colour coded for easy identification: live wire brown, neutral wire blue, earth wire green and yellow stripes.
What happens when a fault lets the live wire touch the metal case of an appliance, raising the case to about 230 V. The earth wire is there to stop this.
Any path joining the live wire to earth, including a person touching the live wire while in contact with the ground. A large current passes along it because there is about 230 V across it.

misconceptions.question: Is the supply at a wall socket in a UK house direct or alternating?
misconceptions.correct: It is alternating: mains electricity is an ac supply, with a frequency of 50 Hz and a potential difference of about 230 V.
misconceptions.misconception: It must be direct, because the socket gives a steady 230 V and appliances plugged into it run steadily.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet dc first with cells, and see that a mains appliance runs smoothly with no visible flickering. A steady effect is read as a steady, one-directional potential difference.
misconceptions.correction: A steady effect does not mean a steady direction. The mains potential difference completes 50 full cycles every second; appliances are simply too slow to respond to each reversal.

misconceptions.question: What changes when a potential difference is alternating rather than direct?
misconceptions.correct: The direction of the potential difference repeatedly reverses, so the current it drives reverses too.
misconceptions.misconception: Alternating means the size of the potential difference goes up and down, but it always pushes the same way round the circuit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'alternating' is read as 'changing', and a graph that rises and falls is described only by its height. Students who ignore the zero line never notice the change of sign.
misconceptions.correction: Look at the zero line on the trace. An alternating potential difference goes below zero as well as above it, and below zero means the push is the other way round the circuit.

misconceptions.question: Which supplies ac, a cell or the mains?
misconceptions.correct: The mains supplies ac; a cell or battery supplies a direct potential difference.
misconceptions.misconception: The cell gives the alternating supply, because chemicals keep moving inside it, and the mains gives a direct supply.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two labels are learnt as a pair of words without being attached to a source, so they are as easily swapped as remembered.
misconceptions.correction: A cell has a fixed positive and a fixed negative terminal, so its potential difference cannot reverse: it is dc. Mains electricity is the ac supply.

misconceptions.question: The UK mains is about 230 V at 50 Hz. Which number is the frequency?
misconceptions.correct: 50 Hz is the frequency; 230 V is the potential difference.
misconceptions.misconception: The supply is about 50 V with a frequency of 230 Hz, or 50 Hz means 50 cycles every minute.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two numbers are memorised as a pair and then reattached to the wrong quantity, and 'per second' is confused with 'per minute' by analogy with heart rate or engine revs.
misconceptions.correction: Hertz means cycles per second, so 50 Hz is 50 complete cycles every second. The potential difference is the 230 V figure.

misconceptions.question: Which wire is brown and which is blue?
misconceptions.correct: The live wire is brown and the neutral wire is blue.
misconceptions.misconception: The live wire is blue and the neutral wire is brown.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both colours are dark and neither has an obvious link to its wire, so the pair is remembered as 'brown and blue' without which is which. Older red-and-black house wiring adds to the confusion.
misconceptions.correction: Use a fixed link: bRown for the Risky wire (live), Blue for the wire that goes Back to the supply (neutral). Live brown, neutral blue.

misconceptions.question: What colour is the insulation on the earth wire?
misconceptions.misconception: The earth wire is plain green, or plain yellow.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Green alone is the colour students associate with the ground and with 'safe', and the striping is a detail that is easily dropped when recalling.
misconceptions.correction: The earth wire is specified as green and yellow stripes. The two-colour stripe is deliberately unlike any other wire, so it cannot be mistaken.

misconceptions.question: Does the earth wire carry a current while an appliance is working normally?
misconceptions.correct: No. The earth wire is at 0 V and only carries a current if there is a fault.
misconceptions.misconception: The earth wire carries current all the time, taking the used-up current away into the ground.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students who think current is used up look for somewhere for it to go, and a wire that runs into the ground is an obvious destination.
misconceptions.correction: The working circuit is live in, neutral out. The earth wire is a safety wire: it is at 0 V and no current passes along it unless a fault connects it to the live wire.

misconceptions.question: What does the colour of a wire's insulation tell you?
misconceptions.correct: It identifies which wire is which: live brown, neutral blue, earth green and yellow.
misconceptions.misconception: The colour shows how much potential difference or current that wire carries, or how well the plastic insulates.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Colour coding is met elsewhere as a scale (resistor bands, hot and cold taps, hazard labels), so students expect the colour to encode a quantity.
misconceptions.correction: The colours are labels, not measurements. The insulation covering each wire is colour coded only for easy identification.

misconceptions.question: Which wire completes the circuit through an appliance?
misconceptions.correct: The neutral wire completes the circuit.
misconceptions.misconception: The earth wire completes the circuit, so an appliance will not work without it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know a circuit needs a return path and know the earth wire goes to the ground, so they merge the two ideas into one wire.
misconceptions.correction: The neutral wire is the return path that completes the circuit. The earth wire is a safety wire, there to stop the appliance becoming live.

misconceptions.question: What is the potential difference between the neutral wire and earth?
misconceptions.correct: About 0 V: the neutral wire is at, or close to, earth potential.
misconceptions.misconception: The neutral wire is also at about 230 V, or the 230 V is shared out as 115 V on each of the two wires.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both wires carry the same current, so students assume they must be at the same potential, or they split the supply pd evenly between the pair.
misconceptions.correction: Potential difference is measured between two points. Live sits about 230 V above earth; neutral sits at, or close to, 0 V, which is why it is the live wire that is dangerous.

misconceptions.question: Is the live wire safe once the appliance is switched off at its switch?
misconceptions.correct: No. The live wire is still at about 230 V right up to the open switch.
misconceptions.misconception: Opening the switch removes the potential difference from the whole circuit, so every wire in it is now at 0 V.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that an open switch stops the current, and then treat 'no current' as meaning 'nothing there'. Potential difference is quietly assumed to vanish with the current.
misconceptions.correction: An open switch only breaks the path. The supply is still connected, so the live wire on the supply side stays at about 230 V relative to earth and can still give a shock.

misconceptions.question: Why is touching only the live wire dangerous?
misconceptions.correct: Your body provides a connection from the live wire to earth, so a current passes through you.
misconceptions.misconception: You are only in danger if you touch the live wire and the neutral wire at the same time, so one hand on one wire is safe.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Circuit diagrams show a loop between two terminals, so students look for two wires and forget that the ground itself is the second connection.
misconceptions.correction: Earth is the other side of the supply. Standing on the ground while touching the live wire completes a path from 230 V to 0 V through your body.

misconceptions.question: What are the three wires in a three-core cable?
misconceptions.correct: A live wire, a neutral wire and an earth wire.
misconceptions.misconception: The three cores are two live wires and a neutral, or a live, a neutral and a fuse wire.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The fuse is the other part of a plug that students remember, and 'three cores' is recalled as a number before the roles of the wires are learnt.
misconceptions.correction: The three cores are live, neutral and earth. The fuse is a component in the plug, fitted in the live wire; it is not one of the cores.

misconceptions.question: What happens if the live wire is connected directly to earth?
misconceptions.correct: A very large current passes along that path, because there is about 230 V across it.
misconceptions.misconception: Nothing much happens, because earth is at 0 V and 0 V cannot drive a current.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 0 V label is read as 'no electricity here', rather than as one end of a 230 V potential difference.
misconceptions.correction: It is the difference that matters. Live at 230 V and earth at 0 V gives about 230 V across the path, and with little resistance the current is large enough to cause burns or fire.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the electricity supply in a UK home?

options.text: An alternating supply, of about 230 V, with a frequency of 50 Hz
options.rationale: Mains electricity is an ac supply; in the United Kingdom it has a frequency of 50 Hz and is about 230 V.

options.text: A direct supply, of about 230 V, with a frequency of 50 Hz
options.rationale: A student who reads a smoothly running appliance as a steady one-way push keeps the right numbers but calls the supply direct.

options.text: An alternating supply, of 50 V, at a frequency of 230 Hz
options.rationale: The two figures have been attached to the wrong quantities by a student memorising the pair of numbers alone.

options.text: A direct supply, of a steady 230 V, with no frequency
options.rationale: Correctly notes that a direct supply has no frequency, but wrongly treats the mains as direct.

mcqs.stem: What is the difference between a direct and an alternating potential difference?

options.text: A direct pd stays the same size, but an alternating pd changes size
options.rationale: Describes only the height of the trace. Size is not the defining difference: it is the direction that reverses.

options.text: A direct pd is always low, but an alternating pd is always big
options.rationale: Generalises from 1.5 V cells and the 230 V mains, treating a size difference as the definition.

options.text: A direct pd acts one way only; an alternating pd keeps reversing
options.rationale: A direct potential difference is always in the same direction; an alternating one repeatedly changes direction.

options.text: A direct pd comes from the mains; an alternating pd from a cell
options.rationale: The two sources have been swapped by a student who learnt the labels without attaching them to a supply.

mcqs.stem: A student connects an oscilloscope first to a cell and then to a low-voltage supply at mains frequency. Which description of the two traces is correct?

options.text: Both traces are flat lines, but the mains line sits much higher up
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who thinks the mains is direct, so both supplies give a steady one-way pd.

options.text: The cell gives a flat line; the mains trace crosses zero
options.rationale: A cell gives a direct pd, drawn as a flat line; the mains pd reverses, so its trace goes above and below zero.

options.text: The cell trace crosses the zero line; the mains gives a flat line
options.rationale: The sources have been swapped: the student has labelled the cell ac and the mains dc.

options.text: Both traces cross zero, but the mains trace is taller
options.rationale: Treats ac and dc as differing only in size, so both supplies are drawn as reversing.

mcqs.stem: The UK mains supply has a frequency of 50 Hz. What does this tell you?

options.text: The pd completes 50 full cycles every minute
options.rationale: Reads hertz as 'per minute', by analogy with rates such as pulse rate or engine revs.

options.text: The supply transfers 50 J of energy each second
options.rationale: Confuses frequency with power, attaching the 50 to an energy transfer instead of to cycles.

options.text: The pd between live and neutral is about 50 V
options.rationale: Attaches the number 50 to the potential difference; the supply pd is about 230 V.

options.text: The pd goes through 50 cycles each second
options.rationale: Hertz means cycles per second, so a 50 Hz supply completes 50 complete cycles each second.

mcqs.stem: Most electrical appliances are connected to the mains using three-core cable. What are the three cores?

options.text: Two live wires together with one neutral wire
options.rationale: Assumes an extra core must be a second supply wire rather than a safety wire.

options.text: The live wire, the neutral wire and the earth wire
options.rationale: Three-core cable contains a live wire, a neutral wire and an earth wire.

options.text: The live wire, the neutral wire and a fuse wire
options.rationale: The fuse is a component fitted in the live wire of the plug, not one of the three cores.

options.text: The live wire, the earth wire and a switch
options.rationale: Drops the neutral wire, from the idea that the earth wire is what completes the circuit.

mcqs.stem: The insulation on the wires in a three-core cable is colour coded. Which row gives the colours correctly?

options.text: Live brown, neutral blue, earth is plain green
options.rationale: Right for live and neutral, but the earth wire is green and yellow stripes, not plain green.

options.text: Live red, neutral black, earth green and yellow
options.rationale: Uses the old house-wiring colours, which students often hear about at home; the cable code is brown and blue.

options.text: Live blue, neutral brown, earth green and yellow stripes
options.rationale: The two dark colours have been swapped over by a student recalling the pair but not the order.

options.text: Live brown, neutral blue, earth green and yellow
options.rationale: The specified colour code: live wire brown, neutral wire blue, earth wire green and yellow stripes.

mcqs.stem: A wire inside a plug is covered in blue insulation. What is the job of this wire?

options.text: It completes the circuit back to the supply
options.rationale: Blue is the neutral wire, and the neutral wire completes the circuit.

options.text: It carries the alternating pd from the supply
options.rationale: That is the job of the live wire; the student has swapped the brown and blue wires.

options.text: It carries current away only if there is a fault
options.rationale: Describes the earth wire, which is green and yellow, not blue.

options.text: It holds the case of the appliance at 0 V
options.rationale: This is the safety job of the earth wire, not of the neutral wire.

mcqs.stem: Why is the insulation covering each wire in a cable colour coded?

options.text: So that each wire can carry a different sized current
options.rationale: Treats colour as a rating. The current a wire carries depends on the circuit, not on its colour.

options.text: Because coloured plastics insulate at a higher voltage
options.rationale: Assumes the dye changes the insulating property; the plastic is the same, only the label differs.

options.text: So that each wire can be identified easily
options.rationale: The insulation covering each wire is colour coded for easy identification.

options.text: So the colour shows which wire is at the highest pd
options.rationale: Close to a real fact (live is at 230 V) but the colour is an identifier, not a measure of pd.

mcqs.stem: What is the job of the live wire in a mains circuit?

options.text: It takes the current back to the supply after the appliance
options.rationale: That is the neutral wire's job; the two supply wires have been swapped.

options.text: It carries a current only if a fault develops in the case
options.rationale: Describes the earth wire. The live wire carries current whenever the appliance is on.

options.text: It stops the metal case of the appliance becoming live
options.rationale: This is the safety role of the earth wire, not of the live wire.

options.text: It carries the alternating potential difference from the supply
options.rationale: The live wire carries the alternating potential difference from the supply.

mcqs.stem: What is the purpose of the earth wire in an appliance with a metal case?

options.text: It is a safety wire that stops the appliance becoming live
options.rationale: The earth wire is a safety wire, there to stop the appliance becoming live.

options.text: It completes the circuit so that a current can pass round
options.rationale: The neutral wire completes the circuit; an appliance still works with the earth wire disconnected.

options.text: It carries the used current away to the ground all the time
options.rationale: From the idea that current is used up and must be disposed of; the earth wire only carries a fault current.

options.text: It supplies the alternating pd to the metal case
options.rationale: Describes the live wire, and would make the case dangerous rather than safe.

mcqs.stem: A kettle is plugged in and working. Which row gives the potential differences correctly?

options.text: Live to earth about 230 V; neutral to earth about 230 V
options.rationale: Assumes both supply wires must be at the same potential because they carry the same current.

options.text: Live to earth about 115 V; neutral to earth also 115 V
options.rationale: Splits the 230 V evenly between the two wires, as if the supply pd were shared.

options.text: Live to earth about 230 V; neutral to earth about 0 V
options.rationale: The pd between the live wire and earth (0 V) is about 230 V; the neutral wire is at, or close to, 0 V.

options.text: Live to earth about 0 V; neutral to earth is 230 V
options.rationale: The roles of the two wires have been swapped, making the neutral wire the dangerous one.

mcqs.stem: When does a current pass along the earth wire of an appliance?

options.text: Whenever the appliance is on
options.rationale: Treats the earth wire as part of the working circuit; only live and neutral carry the working current.

options.text: Only when there is a fault
options.rationale: The earth wire is at 0 V and only carries a current if there is a fault.

options.text: All the time it is plugged in
options.rationale: From the idea that charge constantly drains away to the ground through the earth wire.

options.text: Whenever the current gets large
options.rationale: Imagines the earth wire as an overflow route for extra current, which is the fuse's role, not the earth wire's.

mcqs.stem: A lamp is switched off at a switch in the mains circuit, but is still plugged in. Why can the live wire still be dangerous?

options.text: Opening the switch only lowers the pd to a smaller, safer value
options.rationale: Treats the switch as a dimmer. A switch breaks the path or does not; it does not reduce the supply pd.

options.text: The neutral wire feeds a current back along the live wire
options.rationale: Invents a return path along the live wire; the neutral wire is at about 0 V and supplies nothing.

options.text: It is still at about 230 V relative to earth up to the open switch
options.rationale: The supply is still connected, so the live wire on the supply side of the open switch stays at about 230 V.

options.text: The earth wire raises the lamp's case to about 230 V
options.rationale: The earth wire is at 0 V; it cannot raise anything to 230 V unless a fault has occurred.

mcqs.stem: A person changes a bulb without unplugging the lamp. The switch is open. Standing on a concrete floor, they touch the live contact and receive a shock. Why?

options.text: The earth wire pushes a current out of the ground up through them
options.rationale: The earth wire is at 0 V and drives nothing; the push comes from the live wire.

options.text: The contact is still at 230 V, so a current passes through them
options.rationale: An open switch does not remove the pd, so touching the live contact while on the floor makes a live-to-earth path.

options.text: Their body completes the circuit between live and neutral
options.rationale: Only one wire is touched. The second connection is the ground, not the neutral wire.

options.text: The open switch sends the current out along another wire
options.rationale: An open switch breaks the path rather than redirecting a current somewhere else.

mcqs.stem: A frayed cable lets the bare live wire touch a metal water pipe that runs into the ground. Why is this dangerous?

options.text: No current can pass at all, so the wire overheats and melts
options.rationale: Reads 0 V as 'nothing there'. Heating comes from a large current, not from current being blocked.

options.text: The pd across the appliance rises well above 230 V
options.rationale: The supply pd is fixed at about 230 V; a fault to earth does not raise it.

options.text: The current in the neutral wire immediately changes direction
options.rationale: Current in an ac circuit reverses anyway; that is not what makes this fault dangerous.

options.text: There is 230 V across the path, so a large current passes
options.rationale: Live is about 230 V above earth, and the path has little resistance, so a very large current passes.

mcqs.stem: Why is touching the live wire while standing on wet ground so dangerous, even though only one wire is touched?

options.text: A current passes through them to earth
options.rationale: The body provides a connection between the live wire and earth, so a current passes through it.

options.text: The wet ground stops the earth wire working
options.rationale: The appliance's earth wire is not involved; the danger is the path through the person.

options.text: The pd across the appliance is now doubled
options.rationale: Touching a wire does not change the supply pd, which stays at about 230 V.

options.text: The water raises the pd across them to 460 V
options.rationale: Water lowers the resistance of the path; it does not increase the potential difference.
